youtube.aciklama:
Otoscopy is the first step of every audiological evaluation. In this lesson, we look at the parts of the otoscope, the correct grip and hand bracing, which way to pull the auricle in adults and infants, normal tympanic membrane findings, the light reflex and how to recognize cerumen impaction.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: British Society of Audiology, Recommended Procedure: Ear Examination; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Martin and Clark, Introduction to Audiology; AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guideline: Earwax (Cerumen Impaction).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.baslik: *Otoscopy* Basics: How to Look Inside the Ear
sahneler.alt: Otoscope grip, the auricle and the normal tympanic membrane
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson, we learn otoscopy: examining the ear canal and the tympanic membrane, or eardrum, with a lighted instrument.
Step by step, we will see the correct grip, which way to pull the auricle, the normal eardrum and how to recognize impacted wax.
Otoscopy is the examination of the ear canal and the tympanic membrane with a lighted magnifier.
It is the first step of an audiological evaluation and is done before anything is placed in the ear.
Wax blocking the canal, discharge or a foreign body directly affect test results.
Seeing the ear canal before tympanometry, otoacoustic emission testing or taking an ear impression is a safety step.
After an ear impression is taken, otoscopy is repeated to make sure no material is left in the canal.
The audiologist does not make a diagnosis with otoscopy; any unusual finding is recorded and referred to a physician.

ogeler.metin: The widest tip that fits comfortably

cumleler: An otoscope consists of a battery handle and a head that holds a light source and a magnifier.
The magnifier lets us see the ear canal and eardrum enlarged several times.
The funnel attached to the tip of the head is called the speculum; it is the only part that enters the ear canal.
Choosing the widest speculum that fits comfortably in the canal improves both the view and comfort.
With a bulb attached to some otoscopes, the movement of the eardrum under pressure can be examined; this is pneumatic otoscopy.
For infection control, specula should be single use or properly cleaned after each patient.

yan.metin: If the head moves, the otoscope moves *with it*

cumleler: The otoscope is usually turned upside down, with the handle pointing up, and held like a pen.
The little finger or the side of the holding hand rests lightly against the patient's cheek or head.
This bracing is very important: if the patient suddenly moves their head, the otoscope moves with it and the canal is not injured.
Usually the right ear is examined with the right hand and the left ear with the left hand; the free hand pulls the auricle.
Telling the patient beforehand what you will do reduces sudden movements and anxiety.
As the speculum moves forward, your eye should always be at the magnifier; never advance blindly into the canal.

sahneler.bolum: The auricle and the ear canal

notlar.metin: Inner two thirds: bone, very sensitive

cumleler: In adults, the ear canal is a slightly curved channel about two and a half centimeters long.
Its outer third is cartilage, while its inner two thirds are bone and very sensitive.
To straighten the canal, the auricle, or pinna, is gently pulled.
In adults, the auricle is pulled up and back.
The speculum is advanced only into the cartilage part, slowly and under direct vision; the bony part is not touched.
Touching the bony part can cause pain and, in some people, a cough reflex.
At the end of the canal, the tympanic membrane comes into view.

sahneler.bolum: The auricle and the ear canal
cumleler: In adults, pulling the auricle up and back straightens the curve of the canal.
In infants and young children, however, the auricle is pulled down and back.
This is because the bony canal has not yet developed in infants; the canal is short and made mostly of soft tissue.
This approach is usually used up to about three years of age; in older children, the adult method is used.
In infants, a small speculum is chosen and advanced only a very short way.
The child's head is gently steadied on the parent's lap; sudden movements are more likely at this age.

sahneler.bolum: The auricle and the ear canal
cumleler: Start the examination by looking at the auricle and the surrounding area from the outside.
Note any deformity, redness, surgical scar or trace of discharge.
Starting with the ear without complaints allows comparison and reduces the risk of carrying infection.
After inserting the speculum, first examine the walls of the ear canal.
Then, changing the angle of the speculum slightly, scan all parts of the eardrum systematically.
Ask the patient to tell you at once if they feel pain or discomfort during the examination.

notlar.metin: Pars flaccida (lax part), pars tensa (tense part)

cumleler: The normal tympanic membrane looks pearly gray, translucent and shiny.
Behind the membrane, the manubrium, the handle of the malleus, can be seen as a line running downward.
At the lower end of the manubrium is the umbo, the most retracted point of the membrane.
At the upper end of the manubrium, the lateral process of the malleus, its short process, appears as a small bump.
The small lax area above the lateral process is the pars flaccida, and the large tense remainder is the pars tensa.
The ring-shaped rim that attaches the membrane to the bone is called the annulus.

maddeler.metin: A shift alone is not diagnostic

cumleler: The otoscope light reflects off the membrane and forms a triangular bright area.
This is called the light reflex, or cone of light; it starts at the umbo and extends forward and downward.
That is why the light reflex is seen in the anterior inferior quadrant of the eardrum.
On a clock face, it points to about five o'clock in the right ear and about seven o'clock in the left ear.
The light reflex can shift or disappear when the eardrum is retracted inward or bulging outward.
But it is not a finding on its own; it is judged together with the other features of the eardrum.

yan.metin: A natural secretion that *protects* the ear canal

cumleler: Cerumen, or earwax, is a natural secretion that protects the ear canal and is normally cleared out on its own.
When cerumen builds up and blocks the ear canal, this is called cerumen impaction.
On otoscopy, it appears as a yellow, brown or black mass that covers the eardrum partly or completely.
Hearing is usually not clearly affected unless the canal is completely blocked; complete blockage can cause a conductive loss.
Impacted wax can also disrupt the results of tympanometry, otoacoustic emissions and ear impressions.
In this case, the finding is recorded, the patient is referred to a physician for removal and, if needed, testing is postponed.

maddeler.metin: Small tube in the eardrum: ventilation tube

cumleler: Besides wax, there are other findings you will often see on otoscopy.
A red, swollen ear canal that hurts when touched may suggest otitis externa, an infection of the ear canal.
Discharge in the canal can come from the outer ear or from the middle ear behind a perforated eardrum.
A hole in the eardrum, or perforation, can be noticed by the dark appearance of the middle ear space behind it.
Chalk-white plaques on the eardrum are called tympanosclerosis and are often a sign of a past middle ear infection.
If you see a small tube in the eardrum, it may be a ventilation tube; record this as well.
At the end of otoscopy, the findings are written in the report briefly and clearly.
If the ear canal and eardrum look normal, testing continues.
If impacted wax is seen, the finding is recorded and the person is referred to a physician.
If there is discharge or bleeding in the canal, no earphone or probe is placed in the ear, and the person is referred.
A suspected hole in the eardrum, or perforation, is also recorded; this finding also affects how tympanometry is interpreted.
If a foreign body is seen, do not try to remove it; refer the person to a physician.

sahneler.metin: Use a video otoscope if you can: watching together helps the patient understand the referral, and the recording documents later checks.
cumleler: A tip from practice: use a video otoscope if you can.
Watching the image together helps the patient understand the wax or eardrum finding and why they are being referred.
The recorded image becomes a record for the referral and for comparison at later checks.
For children, seeing their own ear on the screen can also clearly improve cooperation.

maddeler.metin: Otoscopy is the _first step_ of testing
Adult up and back, infant _down and back_

cumleler: Otoscopy is the first step, done before anything is placed in the ear.
The otoscope is held like a pen, and the hand is braced against the patient's head for safety.
The auricle is pulled up and back in adults, and down and back in infants.
The normal eardrum is pearly gray and translucent, and the light reflex is seen in the anterior inferior quadrant.

sahneler.soru: In infant otoscopy, which way is the auricle pulled?
sahneler.aciklama: In infants, the canal is short and soft; the auricle is pulled _down and back_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: When doing otoscopy on an infant, which way is the auricle pulled?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: down and back.
Because the bony canal has not yet developed in infants, the canal is short and soft; pulling upward does not straighten it.
